text: Here's a scenario every quant researcher runs into. You test two hundred variations of a strategy and one posts a Sharpe ratio of two point one. Is that skill? Even if every single variation had zero true edge, pure randomness guarantees some will look impressive just by chance, and you only ever hear about the winner. The deflated Sharpe ratio, from David Bailey and Marcos Lopez de Prado, is built to correct for exactly that.

The core problem is that the expected maximum keeps climbing. If you generate many zero-skill Sharpe ratio estimates, the maximum of that batch isn't centered at zero — it drifts upward as you test more strategies, purely from taking a max over more draws. A Sharpe ratio of one point five might be genuinely remarkable if it's the only strategy you ever tested. The same one point five is completely unremarkable if it's the best of five hundred you tried.

DSR corrects for two things at once. It starts from the probabilistic Sharpe ratio, which already adjusts for sample size, skewness, and kurtosis, because a Sharpe ratio from a short, fat-tailed sample is less trustworthy than the same number from a long, well-behaved one. Then, instead of testing that adjusted Sharpe against zero, DSR tests it against the expected maximum Sharpe ratio you'd see from that many zero-skill trials — a benchmark that rises with both the number of trials and how much their Sharpe ratios vary from each other.

None of this comes from scikit-learn — it's typically hand-implemented. The expected max Sharpe function estimates where the best of N trials would land under pure luck, using the standard deviation of Sharpe ratios across those trials and the number of trials. The deflated Sharpe ratio function then checks the candidate strategy's Sharpe ratio against that inflated benchmark instead of zero, folding in the same skewness and kurtosis adjustment from the probabilistic Sharpe ratio.

A DSR near one says the result would be very unlikely under a pure luck explanation; a DSR near one half or below says the Sharpe ratio you're excited about is exactly what multiple-testing luck would produce anyway. Next, lesson eighteen: detecting backtest overfitting, which ties DSR, CPCV, and purging together into a practical checklist.
